scenarios.name: Game starts with every showroom, vault and score at 0 and round 1
Hand 1 deal: 6 cards set aside and the deck emptied, after one trick each hand holds 9 (counts only, the deal is random)
Hand 3 start (round 21) deals again and the first trick is played (counts only, the deal is random)
The pass gives 2 and takes 2, so every hand is 9 after the first trick (counts only, the deal is random)
Hand 2 start (round 11) re-deals and play goes on (counts only, the deal is random)
Leader may play any card; its suit becomes the led suit and the highest card of that suit wins
A player holding the led suit must follow it; a player without it may play any card
Each player names one of the two other seats as Clubs target, and the trick winner's Clubs action robs that seat
An off-suit action happens at once: seat 2's Hearts crystal is stolen by seat 3's off-suit Clubs
Winning a Diamonds trick adds 1 to the vault
Winning a Hearts trick adds 1 to the showroom
Spades action with a showroom moves 1 crystal from showroom to vault
Spades action with an empty showroom does nothing
Off-suit Clubs takes 1 crystal from the named target's showroom
Off-suit Clubs against an empty showroom does nothing
The highest card of the led suit wins; a higher off-suit card does not
The trick winner takes the led-suit action and leads the next trick
End of hand: a tie on Diamonds gives nothing, the strict Hearts leader gets a crystal and then banks it with Spades
End-of-hand Clubs with tied opponents robs the receiver's left
End-of-hand Clubs robs the opponent with the larger showroom
End of hand: a player who won no tricks gets vault +2
End of hand reveals the set-aside cards; the 6 cards stay set aside and play moves to round 11
Score is recomputed as 2 x vault + showroom
The game ends after round 30's end-of-hand step and the highest score wins

spec_choices.why: The designer fixed 3 seats. The dealer rotation, 'left', the 36-card deal (3 x 10 + 6) and the end-of-hand Clubs tie rule all assume 3 players.

The source has no table talk, and adding it would add a mechanic. Strategy lives in passing, suit play, off-suit timing and Clubs targeting: hold Hearts to build a showroom, use Spades to bank it, and point Clubs at the leader.

spec_choices.what: Card codes such as D7 and seat numbers A=1, B=2, C=3
spec_choices.why: Gives arithmetic a concrete suit letter and rank to compare.

spec_choices.what: The pass is two simultaneous polls of one card each
spec_choices.why: A question returns one choice; two polls keep the pass secret and simultaneous.

spec_choices.what: Every player names a Clubs target with every card, even when Clubs cannot apply
spec_choices.why: The source says every player names one; it is used only if a Clubs action fires.
Vault stays well below 100, so this ranks by score first and vault second, and remaining ties share the win (the draw).

spec_choices.what: End-of-hand suit actions are applied one after another, each seeing the previous result
spec_choices.why: The source says 'for each suit in turn', so a Hearts crystal can be banked by a following Spades action.

simplifications.what: The crystal supply is not tracked
simplifications.why: The source says it is unlimited.

simplifications.what: Each player's turn is split into two asks: card, then Clubs target
simplifications.why: A question returns a single choice.

simplifications.what: Follow-suit is enforced by restricting the offered cards
simplifications.why: Options are filtered from the hand list by led_suit instead of checking after the play.

variation.original_summary: Diamonds is a trick-taking card game for 2 to 6 players. Winning tricks, and playing off-suit when you cannot follow, trigger suit actions that move crystals between a common supply, a public showroom (1 point each) and a hidden vault (2 points each). After 4 to 6 deals, the highest score wins.

review.evidence: Simple policies do not dominate. 'Always play your highest card' wins tricks but throws away off-suit actions and suit majorities. 'Always play low' gives up tricks and the majority bonuses. Choosing when to win, when to dump a Diamond off-suit and whom to rob with Clubs all changes the outcome. A variable player count creates one problem: the seat that leads the first trick rotates unevenly when the number of deals does not divide by the player count.

Card play, voiding suits to unlock off-suit actions, and passing are real skills. But one random 10-card deal per hand decides a lot. With 6 players the 60-card deck is fully dealt and each player has little control, so luck weighs heavily over few deals.

Card counting, planning voids, timing Clubs steals against the leader and fighting for suit majorities give a strong player room to improve. A weak player still collects crystals from tricks and the no-trick consolation.
Opponents' hands are hidden. Players must infer holdings from passes and from who fails to follow suit, and must plan voids over 10 tricks.
The score is crystal counts times 1 or 2. Every action follows mechanically from the cards played.

The game is turn-based and text-only, but it does not fit the limits as written. Up to 6 sequential plays per trick exceeds 4 choice steps. 6 deals of 10 tricks is 60 tricks, over 40 rounds. A variable number of passed cards adds another choice. Clubs targeting is unspecified. The hidden vault is fully trackable from public actions, so it is a memory test rather than real hidden information, and it costs a hidden element.

problems: With more than 4 players, one trick needs more than 4 sequential choice steps, which exceeds the platform limit.
4 to 6 deals of 10 tricks is up to 60 tricks, over the 40-round limit.
Few deals of a large, fully dealt deck let the card draw swamp skill, especially at high player counts.
The first-trick lead rotates unevenly when the number of deals does not divide by the player count, which gives some seats an edge.
The dealer's choice of passing 1 to 3 cards adds a choice step and a rule that is hard to resolve in the engine, for little strategic value.
Clubs steals do not say who chooses the victim or when, and end-of-hand Clubs majorities do not say whom they rob.
The hidden vault is reconstructible from public actions, so it adds bookkeeping rather than inference while using up a hidden element.
Edge cases are undefined: stealing from an empty showroom, Spades with an empty showroom, ties on final score.

changes.what: Fix the game at exactly 3 players.
changes.why: Each trick then needs 3 sequential plays, plus one simultaneous pass poll on deal rounds, which makes exactly 4 choice steps. Three players also avoid the two-player 'only the difference matters' trap: helping or robbing one rival is not automatically good against the other.
changes.fixes: With more than 4 players, one trick needs more than 4 sequential choice steps, which exceeds the platform limit.

changes.what: Play exactly 3 hands of 10 tricks (30 rounds, one trick per round). The deal rotates so that each player leads the first trick of exactly one hand.
changes.why: This stays within 40 rounds and gives every seat the same number of first leads.
changes.fixes: 4 to 6 deals of 10 tricks is up to 60 tricks, over the 40-round limit.

changes.what: Use the same rotation guarantee as above: across the 3 hands, each seat leads the first trick once.
changes.why: This removes the uneven-rotation seat edge.
changes.fixes: The first-trick lead rotates unevenly when the number of deals does not divide by the player count, which gives some seats an edge.

changes.what: Use a 36-card deck (4 suits of ranks 1 to 9). Deal 10 cards to each player and set 6 aside face down and unseen.
changes.why: A smaller deck makes card counting tractable, which rewards reasoning. The 6 unseen cards keep real uncertainty about which cards are live. Three hands, each followed by a pass, let skill average out the draw.
changes.fixes: Few deals of a large, fully dealt deck let the card draw swamp skill, especially at high player counts.

changes.what: Every hand, each player simultaneously passes exactly 2 cards to the player on their left.
changes.why: This keeps the passing decision (voiding suits, feeding or starving the next player) in a single fixed simultaneous poll.
changes.fixes: The dealer's choice of passing 1 to 3 cards adds a choice step and a rule that is hard to resolve in the engine, for little strategic value.

changes.what: Each card play also names a 'Clubs target' (one opponent), which is used if that player gets a Clubs action that trick. An end-of-hand Clubs majority robs the opponent with the largest showroom, with a tie broken toward the opponent on the receiver's left. Stealing from an empty showroom does nothing, and so does Spades with an empty showroom.
changes.why: This makes targeting an explicit opponent-modelling decision (rob the leader, or punish a threat) without adding extra choice steps, and it defines every edge case.
changes.fixes: Clubs steals do not say who chooses the victim or when, and end-of-hand Clubs majorities do not say whom they rob.

changes.what: Make vaults public, and define a tie-break: on equal score, more vault crystals wins; if still tied, the game is a draw.
changes.why: This keeps the 2-point versus 1-point tension (vault crystals are also safe from Clubs) and drops bookkeeping that cannot really be hidden. The hidden information goes where inference is genuine: hands and the unseen cards.
changes.fixes: The hidden vault is reconstructible from public actions, so it adds bookkeeping rather than inference while using up a hidden element.

changes.what: Write out the edge-case rules (empty showroom, Spades with nothing to move, score ties) as part of the rules.
changes.why: This leaves nothing for a judge to decide.
changes.fixes: Edge cases are undefined: stealing from an empty showroom, Spades with an empty showroom, ties on final score.

keeps: Trick-taking with a must-follow-suit rule; the highest card of the led suit wins.

The four suit actions exactly as in the original: Diamonds puts a crystal from the supply into your vault, Hearts puts one into your showroom, Spades moves one from your showroom to your vault, Clubs steals one from another player's showroom.
An off-suit play triggers its suit's action immediately; the trick winner takes the led suit's action.
End-of-hand suit majorities grant suit actions, and ties grant none.
A player who wins no tricks in a hand receives two Diamond actions.
Vault crystals are worth 2 points and showroom crystals 1 point; card passing before each hand; several hands; highest score wins.

recommendation.reason: The core (trick play that unlocks crystal actions, plus Clubs theft) is rich, verifiable and reasoning-heavy. It only needs a fixed 3-player count, a smaller deck, fixed passing and defined targeting to fit the limits and reduce luck.

variation.name: Diamonds: Three-Hand Vault
variation.summary: A 3-player trick-taking game over 3 hands of 10 tricks. Winning tricks, and playing off-suit when void, trigger crystal actions. Players race to fill their vaults, defend their showrooms and choose whom to rob with Clubs.
variation.rules:
COMPONENTS
- A deck of 36 cards: four suits (Diamonds, Hearts, Spades, Clubs), each ranked 1 to 9.
- An unlimited supply of crystals.
- Each player has a showroom and a vault. Both start empty, and the counts of both are public.
- For each hand, the engine tracks how many cards of each suit every player has won, and how many tricks each player has won. These counts are public.

SEATS
- Players sit in fixed order: A, B, C. 'Left' means the next player in that order (A's left is B, B's left is C, C's left is A).

STRUCTURE
- The game is 3 hands of 10 tricks: 30 rounds, one trick per round.
- Hand 1 is rounds 1 to 10, hand 2 is rounds 11 to 20, hand 3 is rounds 21 to 30.
- The dealer is C for hand 1, A for hand 2 and B for hand 3. The player to the dealer's left leads the first trick of the hand, so A, B and C each lead a hand's first trick exactly once.

DEAL AND PASS (first round of each hand only)
1. Shuffle all 36 cards. Deal 10 cards face down to each player. Set the remaining 6 aside face down; no one sees them during the hand.
2. All players at the same moment secretly choose exactly 2 cards from their hand.
3. Each player then gives those 2 cards to the player on their left. Players see their new hand; the passed cards are not announced to anyone else.
4. Reset every player's won-card counts and trick counts to 0.

PLAYING A TRICK (every round)
1. The leader plays any card from their hand, face up, and names one opponent as their Clubs target.
2. The next player to the left then plays a card and names a Clubs target. Then the third player does the same.
3. The suit of the first card is the led suit. A player who holds a card of the led suit must play one. A player who holds none may play any card.
4. OFF-SUIT ACTION: when a player plays a card not of the led suit, they immediately take that card's suit action, before the next player plays.
5. The highest card of the led suit wins the trick.
6. The winner adds the 3 cards to their won counts by suit (each card counts in its own suit) and adds 1 to their trick count.
7. The winner then takes the led suit's action.
8. The winner leads the next trick of the same hand.
9. Everything played and every action taken is announced to all players.

SUIT ACTIONS (for the player taking the action)
- Diamonds: move 1 crystal from the supply to your vault.
- Hearts: move 1 crystal from the supply to your showroom.
- Spades: move 1 crystal from your showroom to your vault. If your showroom is empty, nothing happens.
- Clubs (from a trick or an off-suit play): move 1 crystal from your named Clubs target's showroom to your own showroom. If that showroom is empty, nothing happens.

END OF HAND (after the 10th trick of each hand)
1. For each suit in turn (Diamonds, Hearts, Spades, Clubs), the player with strictly the most won cards of that suit takes that suit's action once. If the top count is tied, no one takes it.
2. An end-of-hand Clubs action robs the opponent with the largest showroom. If those opponents are tied, it robs the one on the receiver's left.
3. Each player who won 0 tricks in the hand takes two Diamond actions.
4. The 6 set-aside cards are then revealed, and all cards are gathered for the next deal.

SCORING
- Each vault crystal is worth 2 points and each showroom crystal 1 point.
- After the 30th round and the third end-of-hand step, the game ends.
variation.objective: The player with the highest score (2 x vault + 1 x showroom) wins. If players tie on score, the tied player with more vault crystals wins. If they are still tied, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Players must count cards across a 36-card deck with 6 unseen cards. They must use the 2-card pass to create voids (so off-suit Diamond dumps become available) without handing the left neighbour a strong suit. They must decide when to take a trick for its led-suit action and when to lose it for an off-suit action, and they must contest the suit majorities. Clubs targeting makes players model the race: robbing the leader helps you and the third player alike, while robbing the weaker player may be safer. Spades lets players bank showroom crystals before they are stolen. Simple policies lose: 'always play highest' wastes off-suit actions and draws Clubs attention, while 'always play lowest' forfeits majorities and still earns the two-Diamond consolation only rarely. With three hands, a pass every hand and one first lead per seat, the deal matters less than play. Talk is deliberately left out. Trick-taking already carries its signals through card play. Open table talk would mostly produce non-binding 'gang up on the leader' calls that no one has to honour. On deal rounds the game already uses all 4 allowed choice steps.

balanced.evidence: VALUE OF EACH ACTION (points to the actor; swing against a chosen rival in brackets): Diamonds +2 (+2). Hearts +1 (+1). Spades +1 if showroom > 0, else 0 (+1). Clubs +1 to you and -1 to the target if the target's showroom > 0 (+2 against that target, 0 against the third player). End-of-hand majority: up to 4 actions, about 6 points, split among players. Zero-trick bonus: +4. TYPICAL HAND: 10 trick-winner actions averaging about 1.4 points give about 14 points. Off-suit actions run about 0 to 6 per player, depending on voids made through the pass. Majorities add up to about 6. One hand is therefore roughly 20 to 26 points spread over 3 players, about 7 to 8 each. NO DOMINANT OPTION: no suit action is best in every situation. Diamonds is worth most, but leading Diamonds hands 2 points to whoever holds the highest Diamond. Discarding off-suit is only possible when void, which depends on the deal and the pass. Leading the suit where you hold the top card wins the trick, but it spends that card and tells opponents what you hold. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE: (1) Always play the highest legal card. You win many tricks but waste high cards on Hearts- and Spades-led tricks worth 0 to 1 point. You never win the zero-trick bonus. Sensible players stay void and discard Diamonds into your tricks, collecting 2 each while you collect 1. You lose often to sensible play and beat random play only about as often as hand strength allows. (2) Always play the lowest legal card. You aim at the 4-point zero-trick bonus but are forced to win whenever your low card is still highest of the led suit, which happens in most deals with 9 ranks. Your scores stay around 4 to 6 against 7 to 9 for sensible play, so you lose most games. (3) Always lead or discard the first listed card. This is effectively random and is beaten by card-tracking play. (4) Always name the leader as Clubs target. This is a political heuristic, not a winner; it only matters when Clubs actions fire. None of these policies never loses. SEATS: dealers are C, A, B, so leaders of each hand's first trick are A, B, C, each exactly once. Passing is always 2 cards to the left, which is symmetric. After the first trick of a hand, the lead follows the trick winner, so no fixed seat keeps the last-to-play advantage. C leads the final hand's first trick with full knowledge of scores, a small endgame edge offset by A leading first in hand 1. Vault and showroom counts are public, so information is symmetric apart from hands. All three players can realistically win. There is no 'higher total makes cooperation pointless' structure: this is a competitive trick-taker, not a social dilemma.

playable.evidence: COMPLETENESS: deal, pass, follow-suit, off-suit timing, trick winner, led-suit action, Clubs target and its empty-showroom case, end-of-hand order (D, H, S, C), Clubs tie rule, zero-trick bonus and tiebreaks (score, then vault, then draw) are all specified. Every player always holds a card, since 10 cards cover 10 tricks. A Clubs target is named with every play, so a Clubs action, whether from leading, winning or discarding, always has a defined target. FINITE: 30 rounds, at most 40. ARITHMETIC: the winner is decided from vault and showroom counts kept by the game; no judge is needed. LIMITS: random draws are 1 (the shuffle) in rounds 1, 11 and 21 and 0 otherwise. Choice steps are at most 4 per round: the pass in the first round of each hand, plus 3 plays, with card and target given as one compound choice of up to 10x2 options. Hidden elements are 2: hands and the set-aside 6. ROUGH STEP COUNT: deal, pass choice, pass apply/reset, play x3, off-suit action x3 (one step each with four `if` ops), winner calc, won-count update, led-suit action, set leader, end-of-hand (sequential `if` ops in Diamond/Heart/Spade/Club order, with a `when` on round 10/20/30), and zero-trick/reveal. This is about 17 to 18, within 20. The first-round deal and pass are single steps gated by `when`, not a conditional block, so this is allowed. Follow-suit is enforced by filtering the option list from the hand. Attributes: showroom, vault, 4 suit counts and tricks per player, plus leader, led suit, high card and dealer at table level, about 14 definitions, under 20. TALK: none, and that is sensible. Three-way politics run through the public Clubs targets and played cards, which players can read from history, so they are inferring, not blindly guessing. A talk phase would add words without changing the trick-taking core. There is no repeated-dilemma late-round problem.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: CHANCE: three random deals of 10 from 36, with 6 unseen. Hand quality, especially holding high Diamonds, varies a lot. Over only 3 hands that leaves about 35 to 45% of outcomes driven by the deal. SKILL LEVERS: (a) Choosing 2 cards to pass, to create a void for off-suit Diamond discards (2 points each) or to avoid feeding your left neighbour high cards. (b) Card counting: 27 cards are visible by play's end, so remaining high cards and voids can be inferred from follow-suit failures. (c) Lead choice, picking suits where you hold the top card and avoiding leads that hand an opponent a Diamond. (d) Ducking toward the 4-point zero-trick bonus when your hand is weak. (e) Racing for end-of-hand majorities. (f) Clubs targeting against the leader, with public scores. ALL-GOOD-PLAY OUTCOME: the winner is not decided by the deal alone. A weak hand can be rescued by passing into a void and discarding Diamonds, or by the zero-trick bonus. A strong hand can be squandered through careless leads. Good play can overcome a bad deal, as in established trick-takers. The game has real hidden information (opponents' hands, the passed cards, the 6 set-aside) and a way to act on what you infer.

design_flags_left: the built game has 8 choice steps per round, over the limit of 4

triage.reason: Every failing scenario fails on `round_number`, which the interface requires to track the current round from 1 to 30. The game never advances it: it stays at 1 after a played round while the file's own `rounds_played` reaches 1. With `round_number` set to 11 or 21 it still ends at 1, so the file overwrites or ignores it. The dealing, passing and trick counts themselves look correct.
triage.guidance: Use the interface attribute `round_number` as the single round counter and drop or derive the separate `rounds_played`. Add 1 to `round_number` at the end of every round, after the trick and any end-of-hand steps resolve, so it reads 2 after round 1, 12 after round 11 and so on. Do not reset or reassign `round_number` in setup or deal steps beyond its starting value of 1. Work out hand start, hand number and dealer from `round_number`: a hand starts when (round_number - 1) % tricks_per_hand == 0, and hand_number = (round_number - 1) // tricks_per_hand + 1. That way a game started at round_number 11 deals hand 2 with dealer A (seat 1) and leader B, and one started at 21 deals hand 3 with dealer B and leader C. Detect end of hand when round_number % tricks_per_hand == 0, and end the game after round total_rounds.

triage.reason: The game advanced round_number after the final trick exactly as it does after every round. The other tests themselves expect round_number 2 after round 1 and 12 after round 11, so 31 after round 30 is consistent behaviour. The ending scenario's assertion of round_number 30 is a check on a turn counter, not on the rule.
triage.guidance: In 'Game ends after round 30; a score tie is broken by vault', drop the round_number == 30 assertion, or expect 31 to match how the counter advances after each round. Instead assert that the game has ended, the final scores and vaults, and the winner. Seat 2 should win the 4-4 score tie on its larger vault (2 vs 1), by the rank_by score*100+vault. Do not assert on round counters or other bookkeeping at game end.

triage.reason: The game was built and behaves as specified, but the design needs 8 choice steps per round, over the limit of 4. The pass is a 2-card selection, and each trick has three sequential plays that each carry a card choice and a Clubs target, so the rules themselves are too complex. Seat results are also somewhat uneven (seat 3: 26 wins, seat 2: 14), which a simpler design should address.
triage.guidance:
Cut the per-round choices to at most 4.
1. Remove the named Clubs target. Make Clubs rob automatically, for example from the opponent with the largest showroom, ties going to the actor's left, as the end-of-hand rule already does. Each trick then needs only the three card plays.
2. Remove the 2-card pass, or replace it with something requiring no extra choice step. If you keep a pass, make it a single card, chosen as one simultaneous poll.
3. Consider shortening the game, for example 3 hands of 6 to 8 tricks with smaller hands, to cut length and complexity.
4. Check seat balance after simplifying. Seat 3 currently does best, possibly because the dealer and lead rotation interacts with the Clubs robbing order. Keep the lead rotation even and make the tie-break for automatic Clubs targets symmetric, for example based on the robbed player's position relative to the actor rather than a fixed seat.
